stories.headline: Houthis Strike Saudi Cities and Energy Facilities, Injuring 73; Riyadh Vows Response
stories.summary:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement launched a major assault Tuesday on four southwestern Saudi cities — Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran — using dozens of drones and ballistic missiles that struck oil facilities and civilian infrastructure, injuring 73 people including women and children. Saudi Arabia's energy ministry confirmed fires broke out at multiple sites, causing a temporary halt in some operations. The Saudi-led coalition called the strikes a "dangerous escalation" and vowed to take "all necessary operational measures" in response.

The Houthis said the attacks were retaliation for more than 120 Saudi air strikes over the previous three days on Houthi-controlled provinces, including a strike on a prison in al-Hazm that the group said killed at least 11 people and left 20 missing under rubble. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the group struck back with "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones" that caused "significant damage."

The escalation is significant in the context of an already volatile regional picture: the four-year informal ceasefire between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began unraveling in July when the Houthis announced a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia and resumed attacks on airports and oil infrastructure. Since Thursday, the Houthis have also launched a new offensive to seize control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

The strikes threaten to widen the Middle East conflict at a moment when U.S. forces are already engaged against Iran in the Gulf and global oil markets are under pressure. Attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and the potential chokehold on both the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab raise serious concerns about global energy supply chains.

stories.headline: Update: New Hampshire Primaries Set Up Pappas-Sununu Senate Showdown in Key Midterm Race
stories.summary:
Rep. Chris Pappas defeated democratic socialist challenger Karishma Manzur in New Hampshire's Democratic Senate primary Tuesday, while former Sen. John E. Sununu defeated Scott Brown and six other Republicans for the GOP nomination. The two will now face each other in November for the seat being vacated by retiring three-term Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, a race widely seen as critical to Democratic hopes of flipping the Senate. Decision Desk HQ and major networks projected both winners on election night.

The New Hampshire Senate race is among the most closely watched contests of the midterm cycle. Republicans view it as one of their strongest pickup opportunities in a political environment that is broadly unfavorable for GOP incumbents; Democrats last won a Senate seat in the state in 2010. Pappas, a moderate four-term House Democrat, fended off pressure from his party's left flank. Sununu, 61, served one Senate term from 2003 to 2009 and carried a Trump endorsement into the primary.

Also on Tuesday's New Hampshire ballot: incumbent Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte easily won her primary and will face Democrat Cinde Warmington in November, and the open 1st Congressional District primary was won by Trump-backed Anthony DiLorenzo on the GOP side. Democrats in the 2nd Congressional District chose between candidates vying for the seat Pappas is vacating.

The results crystallize several of the November midterm's central dynamics: whether moderate Democrats can hold off progressive primary challengers, whether Trump's endorsements translate into general-election strength, and how much the national political environment — including the Iran war and inflation — shapes individual Senate contests that could determine chamber control.

stories.headline: Sudan's Healthcare System on Brink of Collapse as USAID Cuts Close Dozens of Clinics, MSF Warns
stories.summary:
Médecins Sans Frontières warned Tuesday that Sudan's health system is nearing total collapse after the closure of dozens of aid-funded healthcare facilities following the Trump administration's shuttering of USAID, which had been the country's largest donor. MSF said existing USAID grants to many organizations ran out in June, and European governments have simultaneously been reducing international assistance; global aid fell 21.3% in 2025 compared to the previous year, according to OECD data.

Sudan's civil war, now in its fourth year, has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with more than 33 million people requiring medical assistance. In May alone, 45 healthcare centers in central Darfur lost funding and closed. MSF reported that admissions at facilities it supports in central Darfur jumped 22.5% between January and April 2026 compared to the same period the previous year, as patients from shuttered clinics have nowhere else to go.

The practical consequences are severe: pregnant women needing surgical delivery at Gedaref state's Tanedba camp, home to 18,400 displaced people, must now travel three hours to the nearest city after the camp's maternity and surgical wards closed. In Um Rakuba camp, the number of active aid agencies has fallen from 35 in 2021 to fewer than 10, even as the camp hosts roughly 17,000 people, mostly women and children.

MSF urged world leaders gathering at the United Nations General Assembly in New York to take emergency action, warning that without increased support "more patients will face life-threatening situations." The warning highlights a direct humanitarian consequence of the U.S. foreign aid pullback that affects tens of millions of people in one of the world's most acute conflict zones.

stories.headline: UK, France, and Canada Ban Israeli Settlement Goods; Israel Closes British Consulate in East Jerusalem
stories.summary:
Britain, France, Canada, and nine other countries jointly announced on Tuesday a ban on imported goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, calling the move a "turning point" in efforts to reach a two-state solution. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, describing himself as a "proud British Jew," said the government's economic relationships must now reflect its acceptance of the 2024 International Court of Justice ruling that Israel's occupation is unlawful. The bans cover not only settlement products but also companies providing construction, infrastructure, or financing to settlements, along with new restrictions on arms sales.

Israel reacted furiously, with Foreign Minister Gideon Saar delivering what British officials described as a brutal response. Israel announced it would close the UK Consulate in East Jerusalem, which serves the West Bank and liaises with the Palestinian Authority, and removed British representatives from the International Gaza Support Centre coordinating relief efforts in Gaza. Israeli Ambassador to the UN Danny Danon criticized the moves as counterproductive.

Supporters of the bans argue they reflect longstanding legal consensus that settlements are illegal under international law and that economic pressure is necessary to advance a political solution. Israeli officials and their supporters contend the measures are one-sided, ignore Palestinian political dysfunction, and will damage bilateral relationships without advancing peace. Israel's response was seen as particularly fierce given that 12 countries moved in concert, amplifying the diplomatic significance.

The action marks the lowest point in British-Israeli relations in decades, according to diplomatic analysts. With Israeli elections approaching, the heated political atmosphere in Israel may intensify the backlash further. The coordinated Western move signals a potential shift in how European governments are willing to apply economic leverage in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

stories.headline: LIV Golf Files for Bankruptcy Protection with $45 Million Owed to Players
stories.summary:
LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States on Tuesday, citing Saudi Arabia's withdrawal of its multibillion-dollar funding as the primary cause. Court documents show the breakaway golf league owes at least $45 million to players, with two-time major winner Jon Rahm topping the creditor list with an unsecured claim of $7.5 million. Bryson DeChambeau, Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith, and Tyrrell Hatton are also among the top 30 creditors.

LIV estimates its assets at $100 million to $500 million against liabilities of between $500 million and $1 billion. The league says it has secured a new investor in BC Partners and intends to restructure as a majority player-owned entity, with a new version of the league planned to launch early next year. CEO Scott O'Neil said last month he had "high levels of confidence" in achieving a critical mass of players for the new venture.

The Chapter 11 filing effectively voids existing player contracts, with sources saying amounts owed to players and creditors will be addressed through the court process. Players will not be obligated to sign on to a restructured LIV Golf, though it remains unclear when freed players could begin negotiations with the PGA Tour or other tours. Brooks Koepka, who rejoined the PGA Tour in January, still has an unsecured claim of $1.7 million listed in the filing.

Since its controversial launch in 2021, more than $5 billion was spent by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund to establish LIV, which lured top players with enormous contracts and prize money. The collapse raises significant questions about the future of professional golf's competitive landscape and the fate of players who left the PGA Tour to join the Saudi-backed circuit.

stories.headline: Trial Opens in Paris for 14 Accused in Deadliest English Channel Small Boats Disaster
stories.summary:
Fourteen suspected people smugglers went on trial in Paris on Tuesday for their alleged roles in the November 2021 English Channel disaster that killed at least 30 migrants, the deadliest such crossing on record. The defendants, primarily Afghan nationals, face charges of manslaughter and facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organized criminal group. Two alleged ringleaders remain at large and are being tried in absentia.

The boat, described in court documents as "a small boat of poor quality, unfit to navigate at sea, overloaded and equipped with inadequate life-jackets," left the French coast on the evening of November 23, 2021, and began taking on water in the middle of the Channel. Victims one by one entered the frigid water to lighten the vessel's load, and most drowned. Only two of those on board survived; 27 bodies were recovered and four others were confirmed missing. Victims included Iraqis, Somalis, Ethiopians, Egyptians, and Afghans, with the youngest named victim just seven years old.

Defense attorneys argue that many of the defendants were themselves migrants who participated only under coercion from the true organizers. Family members of victims traveled to Paris for the opening of the trial, which is expected to last three weeks. Lawyers representing the families described the smugglers as displaying "total cynicism" and said they took a "deliberate, conscious risk of sending migrants to their deaths."

The disaster also prompted scrutiny of rescue response failures on both sides of the Channel. A UK inquiry found HM Coastguard in Dover was understaffed and that a surveillance aircraft was grounded due to weather, while a widely held belief that migrants exaggerated distress led officials to underestimate the emergency. Seven French military personnel remain under separate judicial investigation on possible charges of failing to assist persons in danger.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Strikes Iranian Tankers Near Kharg Island and Jask in Expanded Economic Pressure Campaign
stories.summary:
U.S. Central Command conducted strikes near Kharg Island and Jask, Iran, on Tuesday, targeting Iranian crude oil tankers with the aim of sinking or disabling vessels central to Iran's export economy, a U.S. official told Fox News. Explosions were confirmed by Iran's state-linked Mehr and Fars news agencies near both locations. A ballistic missile was also reportedly launched from Jask following the strikes.

The strikes are described by U.S. officials as part of a broader campaign — dubbed 'Operation Economic Outcast' — aimed at collapsing Iran's economy by cutting off oil revenue. The Trump administration simultaneously announced 36 new sanctions targeting 27 Iranian airlines and nine foreign entities believed to be facilitating Iranian aviation, including companies with ties to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-linked Mahan Air.

Iran has warned that further U.S. strikes could trigger retaliation against American energy interests in the Persian Gulf. The escalating exchange of strikes has already cost U.S. consumers an estimated $100 billion in higher energy prices, according to earlier analyses, as the conflict — now in its seventh month — continues to disrupt global oil markets.

The targeting of tankers near Kharg Island is particularly significant: Kharg handles the vast majority of Iran's crude oil exports, and strikes there signal a direct attempt to cut off Iran's primary source of foreign revenue. Critics of the campaign, including some congressional Democrats, have questioned the long-term strategy and exit conditions, while supporters argue sustained economic pressure is the only path to altering Iranian behavior without a full ground war.

stories.headline: OpenAI Claims AI Solved Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, but Credit Dispute Clouds Announcement
stories.summary:
OpenAI announced Tuesday that an internal AI model — described as significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra — has produced a proof for the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem, one of seven mathematical challenges designated by the Clay Mathematics Institute as among the most important unsolved problems in the field. A correct, verified solution would be among the most significant mathematical achievements in modern history and could have far-reaching implications for fluid dynamics, weather modeling, and aeronautics.

The announcement is shadowed by a serious credit controversy: outside mathematicians allege that unpublished research they shared with OpenAI's tools may have contributed to the proof without proper acknowledgment. The dispute raises acute questions about whether researchers can safely use frontier AI labs' platforms to explore unpublished work, given the risk of that work being incorporated into the labs' outputs or training pipelines.

The Navier-Stokes equations describe the motion of viscous fluid substances and have resisted a complete mathematical proof of whether smooth solutions always exist in three dimensions. Solving the problem formally would come with a $1 million prize from the Clay Institute, though verification of any claimed proof by the broader mathematical community typically takes months or years.

The episode represents the most dramatic evidence yet that AI is transforming higher mathematics, but also highlights an unresolved tension between AI labs' commercial incentives and the norms of academic science — particularly around attribution, priority, and the integrity of unpublished discovery.

stories.headline: Two Renoir Paintings Worth $10 Million Stolen in French Museum Heist
stories.summary:
Two armed thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer in southern France before dawn on Tuesday, cutting through a perimeter fence and removing four paintings from their frames. Police arrived within five minutes of the alarm sounding at 5:48 a.m., causing the thieves to flee and abandon two works in the museum gardens. Two paintings — including 'Portrait of Madame Romano' (1910) — remain missing, each valued at approximately €9 million ($10.4 million).

CCTV footage showed the suspects wearing helmets, gloves, and combat gear and carrying electric knives and hacksaws, suggesting a professional and premeditated operation. Local Mayor Bryan Masson described the thieves as 'well-equipped and well-informed,' and investigators recovered two zip-up bags believed to belong to the suspects at the scene.

The theft is the latest in a series of high-profile art heists across Europe. Last October, thieves stole France's crown jewels from the Louvre in Paris; last month, four Renaissance paintings were taken from a museum in Sicily. The pattern has prompted renewed calls from museum directors and local officials for governments to fund better security infrastructure for cultural institutions.

The Renoir Museum, which opened in 1960 in the painter's last home before his 1919 death, holds 12 of his works along with personal artifacts including his easel and wheelchair. Mayor Masson called on the French national government to provide greater financial support, warning that museums now face 'a new form of organised crime targeting works of art.'

stories.headline: Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Restore Immigration Verification System Before Midterms
stories.summary:
The Trump administration on Tuesday urged the Supreme Court to reinstate the Department of Homeland Security's overhauled Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system, which is used to check the citizenship status of voters. Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued that a lower court had issued an "indefensible order that threatens the integrity of upcoming elections." It marks the third time the administration has escalated election-related disputes to the Supreme Court, as North Carolina recently became the first state to begin sending mail-in ballots fewer than 60 days before the midterms.

The administration contends the SAVE database is necessary to ensure only eligible citizens participate in elections, framing the lower court's block as a threat to election security. Critics and advocacy groups counter that the push represents what they call a "war" on voting rights, expanding legal challenges against two executive orders on elections they say unconstitutionally supplant state authority over election administration.

The case intersects with broader midterm-season tensions over mail-in voting and voter verification. Advocacy groups, including organizations with veteran election lawyers and former judges, have expanded their legal challenges, arguing the administration's moves are self-serving attempts to reshape election rules close to a federal election. The Supreme Court's response could have immediate practical consequences, as states are already in the process of distributing ballots.

stories.headline: Trump Awards Posthumous Medal of Freedom to 9/11's 'Man in Red Bandana' at 25th Anniversary Event
stories.summary:
President Trump on Tuesday posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Welles Crowther, the 24-year-old volunteer firefighter and equities trader known as the "man in the red bandana" who saved up to 18 lives during the September 11 attacks before dying in the collapse of the South Tower. The ceremony took place during the Tunnel to Towers Foundation's "Steel Across America" event in Washington, D.C., timed to the 25th anniversary of the attacks.

Crowther, a Rockland County, New York native whose father gave him the red bandana as a child, made multiple trips through a barely passable stairwell on the 78th floor of the South Tower, extinguishing fires, directing survivors, and carrying those who could not walk toward the only working escape route. His story became widely known through documentary features and media coverage in the years following the attacks.

The award comes amid a series of 9/11 anniversary events this week, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's release of 170,000 previously hidden documents about toxic air quality at Ground Zero. The Medal of Freedom presentation drew bipartisan praise for Crowther's recognized heroism, separate from the political debates surrounding other anniversary-related actions.

stories.headline: Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch to Retire Amid Clashes With Trump White House
stories.summary:
Smithsonian Institution Secretary Lonnie Bunch III announced Tuesday that he will retire before the end of 2026, following months of escalating conflict with the Trump administration over how the institution presents American history. Bunch, 73, is the first Black leader of the Smithsonian and has been a prominent figure in American cultural and educational life.

The Trump administration has threatened to cut federal funding to the Smithsonian over what it characterized as "ideological activism" in the institution's museums and educational programs. Bunch's departure leaves the Smithsonian facing a leadership transition at a particularly charged moment, as the administration moves to reshape how federally supported institutions interpret U.S. history.

Supporters of Bunch argue his tenure modernized the Smithsonian and broadened its representation of American history, including overseeing the opening of the National Museum of African American History and Culture. Critics aligned with the administration have argued the institution has strayed into partisan territory. His successor will face immediate pressure to navigate the White House's demands while maintaining the Smithsonian's scholarly independence.

stories.headline: Europe Plans to Purchase U.S. Patriot Systems, Send Missiles to Ukraine Ahead of Expected Russian Winter Offensive
stories.summary:
European nations are moving to purchase additional U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems and transfer missiles from their own stockpiles to Ukraine in preparation for an anticipated Russian winter military campaign, Bloomberg reported Tuesday. The effort represents a coordinated European push to bolster Ukrainian air defenses as the conflict enters what analysts expect to be an intensified phase in the coming months.

The move comes days after Russia struck Kyiv, killing two people, despite a recent ceasefire agreement with U.S. envoys, and follows broader stalled peace negotiations that have left fundamental gaps unresolved. European governments are accelerating military support even as diplomatic efforts continue, reflecting concern that Ukraine's air defense inventory has been depleted by sustained Russian drone and missile campaigns.

The Patriot system transfers would require U.S. government approval for re-export, adding a diplomatic dimension to the military logistics. The development also comes as Iran continues to increase pressure around the Strait of Hormuz and North Korea has reinforced positions along the demilitarized zone with South Korea, complicating the broader global security environment in which the Ukraine conflict sits.

stories.headline: NYC Mayor Releases 170,000 Hidden Documents Showing Officials Knew of Toxic Air After 9/11
stories.summary:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani released 170,000 previously withheld government documents on Tuesday, timed to the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, showing that city officials had significant concerns about air quality near Ground Zero even as the public was told the air was safe. The documents, discovered in 68 boxes last year after the city had previously claimed not to have them, were released through an online portal following a lawsuit by advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch.

Among the key documents is an October 2001 memo warning former Deputy Mayor Robert Harding — serving under Mayor Rudy Giuliani — that the city could face up to 35,000 legal claims if health advisories were found to have caused individuals to return to toxic areas too soon. Mayor Mamdani said the documents show asbestos was found 'nearly everywhere' tested near Ground Zero and that 'people got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air.'

Advocate and television host Jon Stewart, who appeared alongside Mamdani at the press conference, said the documents show the city did not recognize the air was toxic until October 2001 — and then kept that information buried for 25 years. The EPA, led at the time by Christine Todd Whitman, declared air near the Twin Towers safe within days of the attacks; Whitman later apologized, saying the agency 'did the very best we could with the knowledge we had.'

Illnesses linked to toxic dust and smoke from the Twin Towers' collapse have now claimed more lives than the attacks themselves, according to U.S. health officials. City Hall announced it will spend more than $34 million on the document release and review effort, with additional documents to be shared over the coming year.

stories.headline: Iceland Summons U.S. Ambassador After Trump Posts Map Showing American Flag Over Island
stories.summary:
Iceland's government summoned the U.S. ambassador on Monday after President Trump posted an image to Truth Social depicting the American flag blanketing Iceland, Greenland, Canada, Mexico, Cuba, and Central America — a provocative visual suggesting territorial annexation of allied and neighboring nations. The Icelandic government called in the ambassador for a formal discussion of the post.

The episode is the latest in a series of territorial gestures by Trump, who has previously pushed publicly for U.S. control of Greenland and floated the idea of making Canada the 51st state. Iceland, a NATO ally and strategically positioned Arctic nation, has not previously been named as a territorial target by the Trump administration.

The White House did not immediately comment on Iceland's diplomatic protest. The posting drew attention across European capitals already on edge following Trump's repeated suggestions that U.S. commitments to NATO allies may be conditional.

stories.headline: Trial Begins in Mexico for Alleged Killers of Australian Surfer Brothers and American Friend
stories.summary:
Three Mexican men went on trial Tuesday in Ensenada for the alleged murders of Australian brothers Callum and Jake Robinson and their American friend Carter Rhoad, whose bodies were found at the bottom of a well in Baja California in 2024 with gunshot wounds to their heads. The men — Jesús 'El Kekas' Gerardo, Irineo Francisco, and Ángel Jesús — face charges of murder, violent robbery, and auto theft, with prosecutors seeking sentences exceeding 200 years each.

The parents of the Robinson brothers traveled from Australia to attend the opening day of the four-week, judge-only trial, issuing a statement saying it was 'incredibly important and overwhelmingly difficult' to be present. 'Callum and Jake were not simply victims in a case file — they were our sons, deeply loved by their family and friends, with lives, dreams and futures that were brutally taken away,' Martin and Debra Robinson said. On the first day, proceedings were moved to a smaller courtroom after reports that witnesses had been intimidated by associates of the defendants.

Prosecutors allege the three tourists were killed during a botched robbery; defense attorneys argued the evidence is insufficient to prove that theory. A former girlfriend of one of the accused was convicted last year and sentenced to 20 years in prison for her role in the killings. Callum Robinson was a professional lacrosse player and member of Australia's national lacrosse team; Jake Robinson had been due to begin work as a doctor upon returning home; Carter Rhoad was killed months before his scheduled wedding.

stories.headline: AfD Wins Historic Saxony-Anhalt Election, Falls Just Short of Outright Majority
stories.summary:
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany party secured 43.8% of the vote in Sunday's Saxony-Anhalt state election, falling three seats short of an outright majority in the 83-seat parliament but recording the strongest result by a far-right party in a German state since World War Two. The CDU, led nationally by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, saw its vote share nearly halved to 17.2%, a result Merz described as "seismic" and said required "profound reforms" from his party.

The AfD's deputy parliamentary leader Beatrix von Storch told the BBC the party was now in talks with other parties and even individual CDU members to form a government, declaring that "democracy demands" its opponents negotiate with it. The state's outgoing CDU premier, Sven Schulze, acknowledged the mandate to govern now lies with the AfD. A minority government arrangement, possibly with tacit support from the left-populist BSW, is among options being discussed.

The result carries significant consequences because governing at the state level would hand the AfD direct powers over policing and education policy. The party's platform for Saxony-Anhalt includes segregating child refugees into separate classes and establishing a task force for detaining and deporting migrants. Germany's domestic intelligence service classifies the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt as "right-wing extremist," a designation the party's state leader Ulrich Siegmund rejects.

The election result is the latest sign of surging far-right sentiment in eastern German states and poses a direct challenge to the long-standing cordon sanitaire maintained by mainstream German parties against governing with the AfD. Analysts and European observers are watching closely, as a governing AfD at the state level would be a watershed moment in postwar German politics.

stories.headline: Update: Russia Strikes Kyiv, Killing Two, Days After Capital Ceasefire Agreement with U.S. Envoys
stories.summary:
Russian forces launched drone strikes on Kyiv in the early hours of Tuesday, killing at least two people and injuring ten others, Ukrainian officials said. Residential buildings were struck in the Solomianskyi district and vehicles caught fire in the Podilskyi district, according to the city's state emergency service. Ukrainian forces simultaneously struck buildings in Russia's Saratov region.

The attack is a significant new development because it came shortly after both countries had agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days during visits by U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv. Russian forces resuming Kyiv strikes within days of that temporary arrangement represents a material collapse of the goodwill measure that accompanied the envoys' trip.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Monday he expects the war to continue into winter following his talks with the U.S. envoys, which ended without a major breakthrough. He called for a trilateral meeting involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States, and officials agreed that U.S., European and Ukrainian representatives would meet again in the near future.

A BBC Verify analysis has found that Kyiv is experiencing more daily air raid alerts than at any point since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022, underscoring the intensification of Russian air operations even as diplomatic contacts continue.

stories.headline: North Korea and Russia Open First Road Bridge Linking the Two Countries
stories.summary:
Russia and North Korea formally opened their first road bridge on Tuesday, spanning the Tumen River and creating a permanent land crossing between the two countries for the first time. Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, appearing by video link at the opening ceremony, called the bridge a "new symbol of friendship" and said ties between Moscow and Pyongyang were at "an unprecedented high level." North Korean Prime Minister Pak Thae Song called it a "historical event."

The kilometre-long structure, visible in satellite imagery since May, can accommodate up to 300 vehicles and 2,323 people daily according to Russian state news agency TASS. Construction began in 2025 following an agreement reached during Vladimir Putin's 2024 visit to North Korea — his first in 24 years — which produced a strategic partnership treaty committing both sides to mutual assistance in the event of aggression against either country.

Ukrainian investigative organisation Truth Hounds said the bridge is intended "primarily to establish a covert military logistics corridor" supporting Russia's war in Ukraine. South Korean intelligence estimates North Korea has already transferred $7 to $14 billion worth of munitions to Russia by sea, and approximately 11,000 North Korean troops are actively fighting in Russia. Analysts say the bridge would facilitate movement of military personnel, construction workers and senior officials in both directions, as well as the flow of Russian technology to Pyongyang.

Pyongyang's official stated purposes for the bridge include "personnel exchanges, tourism and trade." Russian tourists have been allowed into North Korea since 2024, and the Russian government said the crossing will initially carry cargo before opening to passenger traffic later this year. Western governments and Ukraine have consistently raised alarm about the deepening Russia-North Korea military relationship.

stories.headline: Hungary Expels 10 Russian Diplomats for Espionage in Break from Orban Era
stories.summary:
Hungary has ordered 10 Russian diplomats to leave the country after accusing them of conducting espionage activities deemed unacceptable, the Hungarian foreign minister announced Tuesday. The expulsion marks a sharp departure from the accommodating stance toward Moscow maintained for years by former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, whose government consistently blocked or softened EU measures against Russia following its invasion of Ukraine.

The move sets the stage for a direct confrontation between Budapest and Moscow and signals a reorientation of Hungarian foreign policy under the country's new government. Hungary had been widely regarded as Russia's most reliable ally within the European Union and NATO, and Orban's closeness to Putin had drawn repeated criticism from European partners throughout the Ukraine war.

The expulsion brings Hungary in line with actions taken by dozens of other European governments since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, when mass expulsions of Russian diplomats accused of intelligence activities swept across the continent. Details on the specific activities attributed to the 10 expelled diplomats were not immediately disclosed.
